title: Block close: the first thousand years
hook: martyrs, monks, creeds, alphabets, and a church spread across continents

segments.voice: Yesterday: Vladimir's envoys, lost for words in Constantinople, and your line, heaven or earth?

A stadium, packed, rows rising into the dark. Down on the track, one runner, tired, still going. That's roughly the picture the letter to the Hebrews paints. After a long chapter naming the faithful of the past, Abel, Noah, Abraham, Sarah, Moses, Rahab and more, it turns to the reader: "Wherefore seeing we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses." The stands are full. At the end of this block of the path, we look up at them.

This block began with the apostles scattering: they went everywhere. Peter and Paul in Rome. The temple falling, the gospels written down before memories faded. Then the martyrs: Ignatius on the road, calling himself God's wheat; Polycarp; Perpetua and Felicity, a noblewoman and an enslaved woman, sisters in the arena. Christians who stayed in the plague when others fled. Seed, not end. Then a turn: Constantine, a letter granting freedom for all, and the councils. Nicaea and its creed, true God from true God, and Athanasius standing against the world. Then the monks and the builders of mercy: Antony in the desert, Pachomius' community, Basil's city for the sick, Macrina the teacher of teachers, Benedict asking monks to listen with the ear of the heart. Then the long reach: Patrick and Brigid in Ireland, Columba on Iona, Hilda at Whitby, Caedmon finding his song in the stable, Bede finishing his work. And east and south: Ethiopia, Armenia, the Thomas Christians of Kerala, monks with books arriving in China. Ephrem's women's choirs. A dome that seemed to hang from heaven. Icons broken and carried home again. An oak felled, an alphabet made, envoys who couldn't tell heaven from earth. It isn't tidy. There were quarrels, splits, emperors who used the church and Christians who used power badly, and the path has tried to say so. But Hebrews' picture holds. In the letter's image, they're in the stands, and the race is still on. The verse goes on, in the King James words: "let us run with patience the race that is set before us." Tomorrow a new block begins: the middle centuries, east and west, starting with a monastery where the prayer hardly stopped.
screen: then, large: `SO GREAT A CLOUD OF WITNESSES.`

segments.voice: Let the names drift past, Perpetua, Antony, Macrina, Patrick, Bede, Ephrem, Thomas, Boniface, or one I haven't named, and pick the one who stuck, not the most important. Picture them in the stands, watching your race. If you pray, thank God for them by name; if you don't, just thank them, quietly, across the centuries.
Witnesses. The cloud of the faithful dead the letter to the Hebrews pictures filling the stands: apostles, martyrs, monks, creeds, alphabets, a church spread across continents.
Your line: a great cloud. The stands are full, and the race goes on. Day eight hundred six, done.

howItsDone: Christians remember the saints and martyrs of the early church in their calendars, names and churches; Catholic and Orthodox Christians keep their feast days, and some Protestant churches honor them as examples of faith.

chat.says: What does Hebrews mean by a great cloud of witnesses?
options: The faithful who went before, pictured filling the stands while we run our race.
The storm clouds at Sinai, when God gave Moses the law up on the mountain.
The crowd at Pentecost who heard the apostles speak in their own tongues.
